newsitem.title: USA: Doubts about EMU and Japanese comments hurt dollar.
newsitem.headline: Doubts about EMU and Japanese comments hurt dollar.

text.p: NEW YORK, April 18 - The dollar fell on Friday as the mark rose on fresh questions about Italy's chances of being among the first group of countries to form a single European currency.
The dollar also eased against the yen after a senior Japanese financial official warned that the era of record low interest rates in Japan may be coming to an end.

Contradictory reports about Italy's chances of being among the first wave of countries included in the single currency or European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) swept through foreign exchange markets on Friday. The single currency is scheduled to debut on Jan. 1, 1999.

Market News Service cited unnamed officials of the German Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party as saying French President Jacques Chirac was withdrawing support for Italy in its drive to become a founding member of the single European currency. But a source in the French government later denied the report, and Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said Italy wants to be in the initial group of nations.

Any doubts about plans for the single European currency often benefit the mark, which is viewed as a safe haven currency in Europe. Despite the denial and Prodi's assertions, the mark climbed against some European currenices, especially the Italian lira. This, along with the mark's gains against the yen, helped strengthen the German currency against the dollar.

"I think it (concern about Italy) reintroduces scepticism of a broader EMU start, and in general, will raise EMU tensions a little bit," said Bob Lynch, a senior currency analyst at MMS International.

"And given the weakness that we've seen in the deutschemark over the past week, (concern about Italy) provides a little bit more of a reason, I think, to cover short deutschemark positions," Lynch said.

During a news conference on Thursday, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the central bank does not want a weak mark but remains interested in having a strong mark. This statement also continued to weigh on the dollar relative to the mark, according to analysts.
In late New York trading on Friday, the dollar settled at 1.7118 marks, down from 1.7238 marks late Thursday. The dollar fell to 125.88 yen from 125.98 yen.

In an interview with Reuters Financial Television in Tokyo on Friday, senior Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara warned of the danger in assuming Japanese interest rates will remain at record low levels over the coming year.
A hike in Japan's rockbottom official rates could boost the yen by making deposits denominated in the currency more attractive to foreign investors.

Sakakibara, director-general of the Ministry of Finance's International Finance Bureau, also put currency markets on notice that a round of central bank dollar sales for yen was possible if Japanese authorities concluded their currency has fallen too far.
Against other currencies, the dollar slid to 1.4558 Swiss francs from 1.4637 Swiss francs, and eased to Canadian $1.3998 from C$1.4005. The British pound climbed to $1.6330 from $1.6295.
